newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Clintons meet Tutu, praise SAfrica work for unity.
newsitem.headline: Clintons meet Tutu, praise SAfrica work for unity.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton and her daughter Chelsea met with South African Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu on Wednesday and praised him for his role in trying to heal the wounds left by the apartheid past.

Tutu, 65 and a leading campaigner in the struggle against the former racist government, heads the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission -- a body investigating human rights abuses on both sides of the fight.
"I was, as I knew I would be, impressed by the breadth of their efforts and by the seriousness with which (the Commission members and Tutu) have addressed the various issues," Mrs. Clinton said.
She added that the world was watching South Africa try and come to terms with its ugly apartheid legacy.

"I believe that what this Commission is doing is very important not only for South Africa, but for the entire world. So it is something that has a great deal of interest for those of us not directly involved," she said.
Tutu said he was moved by the presence of Mrs. Clinton and Chelsea. "We are very deeply touched by the fact that the First Lady and Chelsea were able to come along," he said.

He said Mrs. Clinton had spoken to him of the importance of symbols in helping the process of reconciliation, citing the United States' Vietnam War Memorial as a way her own country had sought to come to terms with painful episodes of its history.
Tutu said he had noted the advice and a similar project could occur in South Africa. "One of our recommendations is going to be in regard to things of that kind," he said.
But the day was clouded by news that Tutu's prostrate cancer appears to have spread to to other parts of his body and he is now going to the United States for radiation therapy.

However, Tutu shrugged off the news with a joke and said it would not interfere with the Commission's work. Tutu quipped that he had colleagues who were "very, very competent people. I am able to get away and look good because of them."
Mrs Clinton is on the second day of her three-day visit to South Africa. Earlier she visited the Victoria Mxenge homes project and was greeted by crowds of ululating women.

The development is one of many being undertaken in post-apartheid South Africa to try to get proper homes to an estimated one million people who live in poverty, many of them in dense "squatter towns".

The visit to the project emphasised a key goal of her two-week tour of six countries in Africa -- promoting better rights and education for women and children. Of 268 people working at the site, 260 were women.

Mrs. Clinton was led on a tour of the housing project by barefooted Patricia Matolengwe, leader of the South African Homeless People's Federation. A single mother who lives in a shack, she wore a traditional Xhosa costume of bright orange with streaks of white painted on her skin.
Women sang and chanted in the Xhosa tribal language as Mrs. Clinton toured the worksite, where homes were in various stages of construction.
At a welcoming ceremony, a breeze blew dust over Mrs. Clinton, daughter Chelsea and the crowd of 250 or so who gathered around to hear President Clinton's wife.
"I wanted to come and see for myself what I heard about the Federation's work because you are not only building houses, you are building your country," Mrs. Clinton told them.

The women presented Mrs. Clinton with a dark green iron kettle. As Metalongwe presented it to her, she said: "You have to cook something for your husband and we want to know if you cook." Mrs. Clinton smiled and laughed.
